quote: Be vigilant at all times and pray that you have strength.
firstReading: John is shown the river of the water of life flowing from God’s throne and from the Lamb through the holy city. The tree of life bears continual fruit and brings healing to the nations. God’s servants worship him, behold his face, and bear his name. Night gives way forever to God’s light, and the vision closes with Christ’s promise that he is coming soon.
psalmSummary: Psalm 95 summons the faithful to joyful worship before the Lord. They are to sing, give thanks, and acknowledge his greatness above every false god. The sea, dry land, and mountain heights belong to the Creator. Because he is the God who made and shepherds his people, the psalm calls them to bow in adoration and receive their identity as his flock.
gospelSummary: Jesus warns his disciples not to let their hearts become dulled by dissipation, drunkenness, and the anxieties of daily life. Such spiritual carelessness leaves a person unprepared for the day that will come upon the whole earth. He commands constant vigilance and prayer, so that his disciples may have strength to endure what is coming and stand before the Son of Man. The Gospel does not encourage fearful speculation; it calls believers to alert, prayerful fidelity before the Lord who judges and saves.
saintReflection: Saint James of the Marches (Commemoration): Saint James of the Marches (1394–1476) left legal studies to enter the Franciscan Order and became an influential preacher of repentance across fifteenth-century Europe. He promoted devotion to the Holy Name of Jesus, encouraged reform within Franciscan life, and sought reconciliation in communities troubled by violence and division. Some methods and attitudes associated with religious conflict in his period require critical historical judgment and cannot justify coercion or contempt. The fruitful center of his witness is the call to conversion, prayer, disciplined life, and peace under the lordship of Christ. James invites the Church to proclaim the Gospel clearly while respecting conscience and human dignity, to reject prejudice, and to allow devotion to the Holy Name to produce humility, mercy, and reconciliation.
dailyPrayer:
Lord Jesus Christ, source of the water of life and light of the holy city, keep my heart awake before you. Free me from whatever dulls my love: distraction, sin, resentment, and anxious preoccupation with passing things. Teach me to pray with perseverance and to await your coming with reverence rather than fear.

Make me faithful in worship, for the Father has created me and gathers me as one of his people. May the promise of your kingdom purify my desires and strengthen me to endure in hope. Grant that I may seek your face, honor your holy name, and live as one marked by belonging to you.

Through the intercession of Saint James of the Marches, give your Church zeal for conversion, peace, and reconciliation. Preserve us from prejudice, contempt, and every attempt to wound conscience or human dignity. May devotion to your Holy Name form in us humility, mercy, disciplined prayer, and charity. Come, Lord Jesus, and bring your servants safely before the Son of Man. Amen.
theologicalSynthesis:
The readings bring the Church to the threshold of fulfillment. Revelation presents the destiny of grace: communion with God through the Lamb, healing for the nations, worship without darkness, and the vision of God’s face. This is not an escape from creation but its restoration under God’s reign. The psalm answers this promise with adoration of the Creator, whose people belong to him as a flock belongs to its shepherd.

Christ’s warning in Luke gives the proper disposition for awaiting this fulfillment. Vigilance is not agitation about future events, but a sober heart, freed from sin and sustained by prayer. The disciple watches because history belongs to the Son of Man and because every day is lived before his coming.

Saint James of the Marches witnesses to repentance and devotion to Jesus’ Holy Name. His call must be received with moral clarity: Christian proclamation serves the truth in humility, never coercion or contempt. Prayerful conversion bears fruit in mercy, reconciliation, and reverence for the dignity of every person.
exegesis:
Context: Revelation 22:1-7 concludes the biblical vision of the new Jerusalem. John does not offer a merely private consolation or a map of future events; he proclaims the definitive reign of God realized through the Lamb. The life-giving river proceeds from the one throne of God and of the Lamb, revealing that salvation comes from God’s sovereign and merciful presence. Its abundance evokes Eden, yet the vision surpasses Eden: what sin wounded is not simply returned to an earlier state but brought to final communion. The city is holy because God dwells there, and human life is fulfilled in worship rather than self-enclosure.

Context: The tree of life yields fruit continually, and its leaves serve the healing of the nations. This imagery gathers the Church’s hope for a humanity reconciled in God. The curse is removed; estrangement, death, and the rebellion that scarred creation do not have the last word. God’s servants bear his name and see his face. To bear the divine name signifies belonging to God and being configured to his holiness; to see his face expresses the blessed consummation toward which faith journeys. Night is absent because God himself illumines his people. The angel’s insistence that these words are trustworthy establishes hope on God’s fidelity, while Christ’s imminent coming summons the Church to readiness.

Psalm: Psalm 95 supplies the fitting liturgical answer to Revelation’s promise. Israel is summoned to sing, acclaim, and bow before the Lord because he is both Creator and shepherd. The sea, land, and heights are not rival powers; they belong to the God who formed them. Worship therefore is truthful acknowledgment of reality. The Lord is not one force among others, but the maker and ruler of all creation. Yet the psalm’s praise is intimate as well as cosmic: the worshipers are his people and the sheep of his hand. Christian adoration receives this relationship as a gift, not as an achievement. The God before whom the Church kneels is the God who gathers, guides, and sustains her.

Gospel: In Luke 21:34-36, Jesus warns against hearts made heavy by dissipation, drunkenness, and the anxieties of life. These conditions differ in appearance but share a common spiritual effect: they prevent watchfulness. Dissipation turns the heart toward scattered satisfactions; drunkenness obscures judgment; anxiety can imprison the person within concern for temporal burdens. Jesus does not deny the reality of suffering or ordinary needs. Rather, he calls his disciples to refuse any disposition that makes them forget God’s judgment and mercy. The day of the Son of Man comes with universal significance, so disciples must remain spiritually alert. Prayer is not an addition to vigilance; it is its source. By praying at all times, the Church receives strength to persevere and to stand before Christ.

Saints: Saint James of the Marches embodies an urgent call to repentance, disciplined life, and prayer. His devotion to the Holy Name of Jesus directs Christian attention to the Lord before whom all must stand. The name of Jesus is not a slogan for hostility or a possession used against others; it confesses the saving lordship of the crucified and risen Christ. James also sought reconciliation amid violence and division, a concern that accords with Revelation’s vision of healing for the nations. His historical period requires critical moral judgment where religious conflict fostered methods or attitudes incompatible with respect for conscience and human dignity. The Church may receive the fruitful center of his witness—conversion, peace, humility, and mercy—while firmly rejecting coercion, prejudice, and contempt.

Today: These readings call the faithful to live the closing days of the liturgical year in hope-filled sobriety. The promised city teaches that history has a destination in God; the psalm teaches that this hope becomes praise; the Gospel teaches that praise must become vigilant prayer. Readiness for Christ is cultivated through repentance, worship, mercy, and steadfast attention to his presence. It is especially expressed when Christians seek reconciliation rather than division and honor the dignity of those with whom they disagree. Devotion to the Holy Name, as Saint James commended it, bears authentic fruit when it lowers pride, purifies speech, and moves believers toward peace. The Church awaits the Lord not passively, but as servants who worship God, receive his healing, and remain prepared to stand before the Son of Man.
